place: Edge of a small wood, a lone oak standing at a clearing's edge, undergrowth around its base.
lines: chop down the oak with my knife
outcome: A belt knife is far too small and thin-edged to fell a tree of that girth; a sensible person expects only a few shallow nicks in the bark before the edge rolls and the arm tires. After a couple of minutes of hacking the blade is visibly duller and the tree stands untouched but for a scar of pale wood. The knife is now poorly suited even for its usual jobs until it is resharpened.

numbers: how many strikes before the edge dulls
how deep the cut gets

latent: how thick the trunk actually is under the bark
state_after: belt knife: dulled, still in hand
stress: a small tool against a task scaled for a much bigger one
temptation: hardcode that knives cannot cut trees, instead of comparing edge and target size

place: A dooryard woodpile beside a cabin, a chopping block sunk in the dirt.
lines: split this log for firewood
use the wedge and the maul
outcome: Standing the round on the block, setting the wedge in a crack at the end, and driving it with the maul is the right method: after several solid blows the wedge bites deep enough that the grain gives and the round splits clean into two halves. A glancing blow or two miss and just scuff the wedge sideways, costing a little more time, but the split still finishes.

because: oak round is splittable along the grain
numbers: how many blows to drive the wedge deep enough

because: oak round is splittable along the grain
numbers: how much force clears the grain

latent: whether the grain runs straight or is knotted, which decides if it splits clean
state_after: oak round: split into two halves
stress: a multi-step process where each step's success depends on the last
temptation: hardcode 'wedge plus maul always splits oak' instead of checking the grain

place: A gravel bar beside a river, scattered with fist-sized stones.
lines: knock a sharp flake off this flint with the other rock
outcome: Striking the flint's edge at the right angle pops off a thin, razor-sharp flake, useful as a crude cutting edge; a sensible person also expects some strikes to shatter the nodule into blunt chunks instead of clean flakes, and the flakes themselves are sharp enough to cut whoever picks them up carelessly. Here the first strike works and a flake comes free, but reaching for it slices a shallow cut into a finger.

numbers: odds the flake comes off clean versus the nodule shattering
how deep the cut is

latent: whether this particular nodule has a clean grain to flake along
state_after: stone flake: sharp, loose on the gravel
stress: the tool being made is itself dangerous before anyone decides it's a tool
temptation: hardcode flint-knapping as a named crafting recipe instead of deriving it from brittle meeting hard

place: A riverside camp, damp air, a knife sheathed at the player's belt overnight.
lines: skin the fish with my knife
put it away wet
outcome: The knife cuts the fish fine in the moment. But sheathing it wet, without wiping the blade, traps moisture against the steel; overnight the damp does its slow work, and by morning a skin of orange rust has crept along the edge, dulling it and pitting the metal where it sat longest. Nothing shows at the time the knife goes into the sheath.

numbers: how many cuts to skin it
how many hours of damp before rust shows

state_after: belt knife: rusted along the edge, dulled
stress: a consequence that only shows up long after the action that caused it
temptation: hardcode 'knives rust overnight' instead of deriving it from wet plus iron plus enclosure

place: A streamside stand of young willows and one aging birch, no one nearby.
outcome: A beaver gnaws steadily at the birch's base over several nights, carrying off chips to gnaw again later; a sensible person expects the trunk to narrow into an hourglass shape until, on one of those nights, it can no longer hold its own weight and comes down across the stream. Nobody has to be there for it to happen, and nobody chose the direction it falls.

numbers: how many nights of gnawing before the trunk gives
which way it falls, how much of the stream it blocks

latent: whether the birch falls toward the stream or away from it
state_after: birch tree: felled, lying across the stream
stress: world time producing a large change with no player and no call for a region nobody is watching
temptation: hardcode 'beavers fell trees in N days' instead of deriving it from wood loss reducing structural support

place: A quarry face, loose scree at its foot, a stone hammer left leaning against the rock overnight then used again the next day.
lines: break off some stone here
keep hitting it
outcome: A long session of hammering breaks useful chunks free readily enough. But every blow also jars the wooden handle where it is wedged into the stone head, and the wood is drying in the sun between uses; the fit loosens a little each time without anyone noticing. The next day, on the very first swing, the head flies off the handle entirely and the player is left holding bare wood.

numbers: how many blows to break off a usable chunk
how many blows and how much drying before the head is loose
odds the head comes free on a given swing

latent: how loose the fit has actually gotten, unseen inside the haft
state_after: stone hammer: head detached, handle bare
stress: wear accumulating unseen across uses until a routine action fails suddenly
temptation: hardcode 'tools break after N uses' instead of deriving wear from repeated stress plus a drying material

place: A campfire clearing, a length of green willow branch and a whittling knife.
lines: carve a spoon out of this branch
outcome: Green wood carves easily along the grain, and the bowl of a spoon starts to take shape in a few minutes of steady cutting. Cutting across the grain near a knot catches the blade and the wood splits away in a long crack instead of shaving off cleanly, ruining the spoon's handle; a curl of wood also flicks off and lodges as a splinter under a thumbnail. A sensible person would have to start the handle over from a straighter section.

numbers: how many passes to shape the bowl

because: willow branch is splittable along the grain
numbers: odds the cut catches a knot

latent: where the hidden knot inside the branch actually is
state_after: willow branch: partly carved, cracked handle
stress: grain direction deciding success at a scale as small as a splinter
temptation: hardcode carving as a single success roll instead of deriving grain, knots and splinters

place: A half-built fence line at the edge of a field, posts driven, no mallet on hand.
lines: I don't have a mallet, use a rock to drive this peg in
outcome: A rock is a poor substitute for a mallet: heavy and hard enough to drive the peg, but with no handle and an irregular face it is harder to aim, so a sensible person expects it to take more swings and land a few glancing blows that skid off and bruise knuckles or dent the peg's top instead of driving it. The peg does go in by the end, crooked and a little mushroomed at the head.

because: wooden peg is softer than stone
numbers: how many swings, how many miss cleanly

state_after: wooden peg: driven in, crooked, head mushroomed
stress: an improvised tool that works but worse, not a binary pass or fail
temptation: hardcode 'pegs need a mallet' instead of deriving the result from weight, hardness and grip

place: A quarry ledge in late autumn, a fissured boulder sitting where rain pools in a crack overnight, a cold snap coming.
outcome: Rain fills a hairline crack in the boulder during the day; overnight the cold snap freezes the water, and ice takes up more room than water did, so the crack is forced wider. A sensible person expects this to take several freezing nights, not one, but by the third morning the boulder has split clean along the widened crack with nobody near it. The pieces sit ready to be worked, if anyone comes looking.

numbers: how many freeze-thaw nights before the crack widens enough
how wide the crack gets, how many pieces result

latent: whether the crack was deep enough to split the boulder all the way through
state_after: fissured boulder: split into two pieces
stress: a purely physical process running over days with no creature or player involved at all
temptation: hardcode 'boulders crack in freezing weather' instead of deriving it from water in a crack expanding when it freezes

place: A campsite, a coil of old hemp rope needing to be cut to length, only a badly blunted knife at hand.
lines: cut the rope
outcome: A blade with no edge left cannot part rope fibers cleanly; a sensible person expects sawing back and forth to fray and mash the strands rather than sever them, wasting time and leaving a ragged, weakened end instead of a clean cut. After a long effort a few outer fibers finally give, but the rope is still one piece, just frayed and harder to tie with.

numbers: how long the sawing takes for how little result

state_after: hemp rope: frayed at one end, not severed
stress: an action that visibly does something but does not achieve its goal
temptation: hardcode a yes-or-no check for whether a knife cuts rope, instead of comparing edge condition to material toughness

place: A shallow stream cutting through a meadow, banks about four strides apart, a stand of straight young trees nearby.
lines: build a bridge
outcome: 'Build a bridge' with no plan given still needs a sensible person to fell trunks long enough to span the banks, drag them across, and lash them together so they do not roll apart; a loose deck of unlashed logs would just spread and dump anyone crossing. Here the player drags three trunks over and lashes them at both ends, which holds a walking load, but the middle sags noticeably underfoot and would not take a laden cart.

numbers: how long the drag takes for trunks this size
whether the span reaches both banks
how much rope the lashing uses, how much load the lashing holds

latent: whether the far bank is firm enough to anchor the logs or crumbles under weight
state_after: log span: crossable but sagging in the middle
coil of rope: mostly used up
stress: a vague, overambitious command that a sensible person still has to break into real steps
temptation: hardcode a single 'build bridge' verb instead of deriving it from drag, span and bind

place: A dirt trail, a loaded sled being pulled behind the player over rough, rutted ground.
lines: tie the load down with this rope and drag the sled
outcome: A rope thrown over the load and knotted quickly, without a real hitch, holds while the ground is smooth; a sensible person expects a poor knot to work loose exactly when it is tested hardest. Partway down the rutted trail a jolt shakes the knot enough that it slips, and the sack of grain rolls off the sled into the mud, spilling some grain before the player notices.

numbers: how secure the knot is, from how it was tied
how much jolting the ruts cause
how much grain is lost

state_after: sack of grain: on the ground, torn open, part spilled
rope: loose, still attached to sled
stress: a knot's quality only shows under the stress that comes later, not when it is tied
temptation: hardcode that tying an item just needs rope present, with no check on how well the knot is made

place: A field with a half-buried boulder blocking a planned furrow, a slender fence rail lying nearby.
lines: pry this boulder out with the fence rail
outcome: A lever can move a boulder this size, but only if the beam is stout enough to take the bending force; a thin fence rail is the wrong scale of tool for a boulder this heavy. Wedged under the rock and heaved on, the rail bows and then snaps clean across partway through the push, and the boulder does not budge.

numbers: how much force the rail can take before it fails, versus how much the boulder needs

latent: exactly how deep the boulder is buried, and so how much force moving it would take
stress: a lever's own strength as the limiting factor, not the effort put into it
temptation: hardcode 'levers move heavy things' instead of comparing beam strength to load

place: A rocky slope being cleared for a garden plot, loose stones piled to one side, a rabbit hutch propped nearby.
lines: stack these stones into a wall here
outcome: Stacking flat stones without stepping the courses inward keeps the wall going up easily at first, but a sensible person expects a tall, straight-sided stack of ungraded stones to grow unstable past chest height. Here the stack topples once it gets too tall for its base, and the fall is not contained to the wall: two stones bounce wide and crack the side of the rabbit hutch that happened to be sitting close by.

numbers: how tall the stack gets before it is unstable
how far the falling stones scatter
odds a scattering stone reaches something nearby

latent: how stable the ground under the wall's base actually is
state_after: rabbit hutch: cracked on one side
loose stones: spread across the slope
stress: a collapse whose debris reaches something the player never meant to involve
temptation: hardcode that walls fall after a fixed number of stones instead of deriving stability from base width versus height

place: An open-sided lean-to shelter, its frame lashed together with rawhide cord, left through two days of steady rain with nobody there.
outcome: Rawhide cord swells and softens when it stays wet, and the steady rain soaks every lashing on the frame over the two days; a sensible person expects the joints to loosen as the cord loses its grip, though nothing actually gives way yet since nothing has stressed the frame while it is wet. By the time anyone returns, the whole structure sways at a touch, one strong gust away from coming down, though it is still standing.

numbers: how many hours of rain before the lashings loosen

stress: damage that accumulates over unobserved time with nothing failing outright yet
temptation: hardcode that shelters need repair every fixed number of days instead of deriving looseness from a wet binding material

place: A trapline at the edge of the woods, a snare set the day before, staked to the ground with a cord running to a bent sapling.
outcome: A fox passing in the night finds the cord underfoot before ever touching the loop meant to catch it, and a sensible person expects a hungry animal to gnaw at anything unfamiliar snagging its foot rather than pull free cleanly. It chews through the cord and wanders off unharmed; the sapling springs upright with nothing caught, and the trap has to be reset before it will work again.

because: fox is caught by the foot
numbers: how long it takes to chew through

stress: a trap defeated by the very animal it was set for, with nobody watching
temptation: hardcode that traps catch prey after a fixed number of hours instead of letting a caught animal act on the trap itself

place: A low cliff face beside a dry riverbed, a dead branch jutting out partway up, used as a handhold.
lines: climb up using that branch
outcome: A dead branch looks like a handhold but rot has hollowed it out inside where nothing shows from the outside; a sensible person's weight on it is exactly the kind of load that finds a hidden weakness. It snaps the moment full weight comes onto it, and the player drops the short distance already climbed, landing hard on the riverbed stones. Nothing is broken, but the fall bruises badly enough that walking is stiff and slow for the rest of the day.

numbers: odds the rot is enough to fail under this weight

because: cliff face is above the riverbed
numbers: how far the fall is, how hard the landing

latent: that the branch is hollow with rot, invisible until it is loaded
state_after: dead branch: snapped, hanging by a strip of bark
cliff face: partly climbed, handhold gone
stress: a hidden flaw that only a real load reveals, with a consequence lasting past the moment
temptation: hardcode that branches are safe handholds instead of deriving hidden rot from exposure and age

place: A game trail through brush at the woods' edge, a flat rock and a springy sapling nearby.
lines: set a deadfall trap here
prop the rock up with a stick over the trail
outcome: Propping a heavy flat rock at a steep angle on a thin trigger stick, balanced so the lightest touch on the trail knocks the stick free, is a workable trap if the prop is set right; a sensible person expects most of the waiting to happen with nothing around to trigger it. Set at dusk, the trap sits untouched through the night and into the next day, until a foraging grouse finally brushes the trigger toward evening and the rock comes down, catching it.

numbers: how precarious the balance is, and so how light a touch trips it

because: trigger stick crosses the game trail
game trail is used by grouse
numbers: how long before something crosses the trail
odds the fall lands on the grouse rather than beside it

latent: whether anything at all crosses this stretch of trail before the trap is checked
state_after: flat rock: fallen, resting on the trail
stress: a trap whose whole point is to act on its own after the player has walked away
temptation: hardcode that traps catch food after a fixed number of hours instead of deriving the wait from something actually crossing the trail

place: A clearing with a wild apple tree, fruit hanging out of reach, and a wasp nest tucked in the branches above it that is not visible from the ground.
lines: throw a rock up to knock some apples down
outcome: Throwing a rock into a branch to shake fruit loose is a reasonable improvisation and does knock two apples down; a sensible person has no way to know a wasp nest is tucked further up the same tree until the rock's impact rattles those branches too. The nest is jarred hard enough to send wasps pouring out, and the player has to run from the clearing without the apples they just knocked down.

because: apple tree's fruit is out of reach
fist-sized rock is heavy enough to shake a branch
numbers: how many apples come loose

because: hidden wasp nest is near the impact

numbers: how many wasps, how many stings before the player is clear

latent: the wasp nest, unseen from the ground until it is already disturbed
state_after: fallen apples: on the ground, unclaimed
hidden wasp nest: agitated, wasps out
stress: an unrelated hazard triggered as a side effect of an ordinary action
temptation: hardcode that wasp nests sting when found instead of letting any disturbance nearby reach a hidden thing

place: A fallen log at the treeline, branches propped against it to make a lean-to shelter, first light snowfall of the season starting that evening.
lines: prop branches against the log for a shelter
outcome: Leaning a course of branches against the log at a steep angle sheds rain fine and holds its shape the first night; a sensible person expects a light roof like this to take some load before failing, not none. Snow falls steadily for two days while the player is elsewhere in the clearing, building up on the branches faster than it slides off the shallow pitch, and on the second night the accumulated weight finally bows the branches past their limit and the roof caves in.

numbers: how steep the pitch is
how much snow piles up over two days
how much weight the branches could take before failing

latent: how steep the pitch really is, which decides whether snow slides off or piles up
state_after: snow: piled where the roof used to be
stress: a structure that is fine under one load, tested slowly to failure by an accumulating one
temptation: hardcode that shelters last a fixed number of days instead of deriving collapse from load building up against a strength limit
